newsitem.title: USA: Europe must cut budget deficits more - IMF official.
newsitem.headline: Europe must cut budget deficits more - IMF official.

text.p: By Rich Miller, Economics Correspondent

Germany, France and Italy need to do more to cut their budget deficits to meet tough criteria for inclusion in European monetary union, but all seem determined to do so, a senior IMF official said Monday.

"We know that certainly there is something more to do there (in Italy) as there is certainly something more to do in Germany, certainly more to do in France and in several others," the International Monetary Fund official said.
Speaking to reporters ahead of this week's semi-annual meeting of the IMF and World Bank, the official was upbeat about the outlook for the world economy.
"We have rather good news about how things are developing in the world," he said, in apparent reference to IMF forecasts for solid global growth this year
The United States in particular has done well, said the official, who declined to be identified.

It needs to continue to keep inflation in check -- the recent rise in interest rates by the Federal Reserve should help in that regard -- and to further reduce its federal government budget deficit in the medium term, he added.
"It is proceeding in its moderate strengthening of monetary conditions," the official said, in apparent reference to the U.S. central bank.

The official acknowledged that Europe could be seen as a "black spot" for the world economy in 1997. But he argued that the drive to launch a single currency there was good in both the short- and long-run.

Under the Maastricht treaty, European countries must reduce their budget deficits this year toward the equivalent of 3 percent of gross domestic product to participate in monetary union when the euro, as the new currency is to be known, is introduced in 1999.
The senior IMF official urged European countries to press ahead with the efforts to bring their budget deficits down and restructure their economies.
"What the European nations must do now is to forget their doubts and hesitations and finish the job," he said.
"The conditions for the successful start of the euro are largely in place," he added, noting that Europe is now infused with a "culture of stability," including low inflation.

The IMF official called the determination of Germany, France and "most notably" Italy to press ahead "impressive," noting that Rome is seeking to slash its budget deficit from the equivalent of 7 percent of GDP last year.

He said he was convinced that Italy was serious about taking additional structural measures to improve its budget position this year and in the long-run. In particular, he highlighted the importance of further pension reforms.
"Everybody knows that they (Italy) will take additional measures," the official added.
He also stressed the importance of all European countries continuing to cut their deficits after 1997, even to the point of eliminating them.
While extolling the benefits of monetary union for Europe and the world economy, the IMF official said the launch of the euro could lead to some instability in currency markets.
"It could be accompanied by a certain degree of instability in the exchange market," he said.

That would come about because of a move away from an international monetary system dominated by one currency -- the U.S. dollar -- to bipolar or possibly tripolar one, where the euro and perhaps the Japanese yen would play a greater role.
"We must be prepared to face that," the senior IMF official said.
